body: Why did the librarian propose discussing a few notes with students before deciding whether to continue the programme?
options: To add evidence about students’ experience to the numerical return record.
To grade every note before including it in the borrowing totals.
To verify that book returns continued to rise in the fourth week.
To determine whether students could borrow more than two books at a time.
explanation: The return records showed when books were returned, but not how carefully they had been read. Discussing notes with students would add evidence about their experience before the librarian decided whether to continue the programme.
passage_text: In a fictional school library, a trial reading programme ran for four weeks. Students could borrow two books at a time. Each Friday they returned at least one book and wrote a short note about it. The librarian recorded the number of books returned, but did not grade the notes. At the end of the trial, the borrowing records showed an increase in returns during the second and third weeks, followed by a small decrease in the fourth. The librarian said the records showed when books were returned, rather than how carefully they had been read. She proposed discussing a few notes with students before deciding whether to continue the programme. The proposal therefore combined a numerical record with evidence about the students’ experience.
evidence_quotes: The librarian said the records showed when books were returned, rather than how carefully they had been read.
She proposed discussing a few notes with students before deciding whether to continue the programme.
The proposal therefore combined a numerical record with evidence about the students’ experience.

B is incorrect: the passage says the librarian did not grade the notes.
C is incorrect: the passage says returns decreased slightly in the fourth week.
D is incorrect: the passage states that students could borrow two books at a time, and the proposed discussion concerned notes.

body:
Match List-I with List-II. Each entry in List-I is to be matched with one entry in List-II, and each entry in List-II is to be used once.

List-I
(A) Benevolent
(B) Candid
(C) Coherent
(D) Concise

List-II
(I) Giving only the information that is necessary and important, using few words
(II) Logical and well organised; easy to understand and clear
(III) Kind, helpful and generous
(IV) Saying what you think openly and honestly; not hiding your thoughts

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Benevolent means kind, helpful and generous, while candid describes speaking openly and honestly. Coherent means logical and well organised, and concise means giving necessary information in few words. These meanings give the one-to-one mapping in option C.

body: Assume that a report’s key findings are the only information necessary and important. Choose the sentence in which “concise” is used correctly to mean giving only necessary and important information, using few words.
options: The writer described the report as concise because it included every detail, whether important or not.
The writer described the report as concise because it omitted one of its key findings and retained minor details.
The writer described the report as concise because it retained its key findings and used few words.
The writer described the report as concise because it expanded each point with lengthy, unrelated explanations.
explanation: Concise means giving only necessary and important information using few words. The stem identifies the key findings as the report’s necessary and important information, and option C says these are retained and expressed using few words. The other options include minor details, omit a key finding, or add lengthy unrelated explanations.
evidence_quotes: giving only the information that is necessary and important, using few words
stated_assumptions: The report’s key findings are the only information necessary and important.
The descriptions of the reports in the options are accurate.
option_analysis: A is incorrect because it includes every detail, including details that are not important.
B is incorrect because it omits a key finding and retains minor details.
C is correct because it retains the necessary and important information and uses few words.
D is incorrect because it adds lengthy, unrelated explanations.

body: Why did Mira remain at the workshop until the radio’s wooden case was ready?
options: To give the electrical work enough time to be completed
To wait until the rain stopped before travelling
To let the wooden case dry and avoid damaging its finish
To ask her grandfather to repair the radio himself
explanation: The repairer had finished the electrical work but warned that carrying the radio before the case dried could spoil its finish. Mira stayed until the case was ready, then carried the radio home.
passage_text: Mira had promised to bring her grandfather’s repaired radio home before sunset. At the workshop she found that the repairer had finished the electrical work, but the wooden case still needed to dry. “It will play,” he said, “but carrying it now may spoil the finish.” Mira looked at the dark clouds and then at the road to her village. She could reach home in time if she left immediately. Instead, she telephoned her grandfather and explained the delay. “A promise includes care,” he replied. She sat beside the workshop window until the case was ready. On the journey home the rain began, and she covered the radio with her coat. When she arrived, her grandfather switched it on. Neither of them mentioned the missed sunset; they listened quietly to the music.
evidence_quotes: “It will play,” he said, “but carrying it now may spoil the finish.”
She sat beside the workshop window until the case was ready.
stated_assumptions: The supplied narrative is the source for the events in the question.
The question asks why Mira stayed at the workshop, rather than asking about her later journey home.
option_analysis: Incorrect: the narrative says the repairer had already finished the electrical work.
Incorrect: the rain began on the journey home, after Mira left the workshop.
Correct: the case still needed to dry, and carrying the radio before then could spoil its finish.
Incorrect: the repairer was doing the work, and the narrative gives no indication that Mira stayed to ask her grandfather to repair the radio.

body:
Arrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
(A) This identification illustrates the two-part structure stated at the beginning.
(B) In it, “He” is the noun phrase (subject), while “acceded to demands for his resignation” is the verb phrase.
(C) All clauses in English have at least two parts: a noun phrase (subject) and a verb phrase.
(D) For instance, consider the clause “He acceded to demands for his resignation.”
Choose the correct sequence from the options given below:
explanation: Sentence (C) introduces the two-part structure, and sentence (D) then presents an example. In sentence (B), “In it” refers to the clause introduced in (D) and identifies its noun phrase and verb phrase. Sentence (A) follows that identification and refers back to the structure stated at the beginning.
evidence_quotes: All clauses in English have at least two parts, a noun phrase (subject) and a verb phrase
He acceded to demands for his resignation.
stated_assumptions: The four labelled sentences are intended to form one short explanatory paragraph.
In sentence (B), “In it” refers to the clause introduced in sentence (D); in sentence (A), “This identification” refers to the identification in sentence (B).
option_analysis: A is incorrect because sentence (B) refers to the example in (D), while sentence (C), which is said to be stated at the beginning, would come after them.
B is incorrect because “In it” in sentence (B) appears before the clause it refers to in sentence (D).
C is incorrect because “This identification” in sentence (A) appears before the identification in sentence (B).
D is correct: sentence (C) states the structure, (D) gives the example, (B) identifies its two parts, and (A) closes the explanation.

body: A company reports an inventory turnover ratio of 6 times for an accounting period. What does this figure mean?
options: Inventory was converted into revenue from operations six times during the period.
Inventory amounted to 6 per cent of revenue from operations during the period.
Average inventory was six times the cost of revenue from operations during the period.
Inventory remained in stock for an average of six days during the period.
explanation: Inventory turnover ratio indicates the number of times inventory is converted into revenue from operations during the accounting period. Therefore, a ratio of 6 times means that this conversion occurred six times.
evidence_quotes: It determines the number of times inventory is converted into revenue from operations during the accounting period under consideration.
stated_assumptions: The reported figure is the inventory turnover ratio for the stated accounting period.
option_analysis: A: Correct. It directly expresses the stated meaning of inventory turnover ratio.

body: Four existing partners, A, B, C and D, share profits in the ratio 1/2 : 1/4 : 1/6 : 1/12. They change their profit-sharing ratio to 13/30 : 3/20 : 13/60 : 1/5, with no partner admitted or retiring. What are the sacrificing ratio A:B and the gaining ratio C:D?
options: Sacrificing ratio A:B = 3:2, and gaining ratio C:D = 7:3
Sacrificing ratio A:B = 2:3, and gaining ratio C:D = 3:7
Sacrificing ratio A:B = 2:3, and gaining ratio C:D = 7:3
Sacrificing ratio A:B = 3:2, and gaining ratio C:D = 3:7
explanation: A's and B's shares decrease by 1/2 − 13/30 = 1/15 and 1/4 − 3/20 = 1/10, respectively, so their sacrificing ratio is 2:3. C's and D's shares increase by 13/60 − 1/6 = 1/20 and 1/5 − 1/12 = 7/60, respectively, so their gaining ratio is 3:7.
evidence_quotes: Sometimes, the partners of a firm decide to change their existing profit sharing ratio without any admission or retirement of a partner. This results in a gain of additional share in future profits of the firm for some partners while a loss of a part thereof for other partners.
stated_assumptions: A, B, C and D are the existing partners, and no partner is admitted or retires.
The old shares are A = 1/2, B = 1/4, C = 1/6 and D = 1/12 of the same total profits.
The new shares are A = 13/30, B = 3/20, C = 13/60 and D = 1/5 of that same total profits.
option_analysis: A reverses both calculated ratios: the sacrifices are A:B = 2:3, not 3:2, and the gains are C:D = 3:7, not 7:3.
B correctly compares each partner's old and new share: A and B sacrifice in the ratio 2:3, while C and D gain in the ratio 3:7.
C reverses the calculated gaining ratio; C:D is 3:7, not 7:3.
D reverses the calculated sacrificing ratio; A:B is 2:3, not 3:2.

body:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Assess current profitability and operational efficiency to judge the firm’s financial health.
(B) Ascertain the relative importance of components of the firm’s financial position.
(C) Identify reasons for a change in profitability or financial position.
(D) Judge the firm’s ability to repay debt and assess its short-term and long-term liquidity.

List-II
(I) Which components have greater or lesser importance in the firm’s financial position?
(II) What explains the change in the firm’s profitability or financial position?
(III) How able is the firm to repay debt, and what is its short-term and long-term liquidity position?
(IV) How profitable and operationally efficient is the firm, overall and across its departments, for judging its financial health?

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Option D matches each purpose with the question it addresses: current profitability and operational efficiency with IV, relative importance of components with I, reasons for change with II, and debt repayment and liquidity with III. The stated purposes distinguish these four objectives.
evidence_quotes: to assess the current profitability and operational efficiency of the firm as a whole as well as its different departments so as to judge the financial health of the firm.
to ascertain the relative importance of different components of the financial position of the firm.
to identify the reasons for change in the profitability/financial position of the firm.
to judge the ability of the firm to repay its debt and assessing the short-term as well as the long-term liquidity position of the firm.
stated_assumptions: Each List-II item is to be matched to the financial-analysis purpose it describes.
option_analysis: Incorrect: it assigns the purpose of ascertaining relative importance to a question about reasons for change, and the purpose of identifying reasons for change to a question about relative importance.

Incorrect: it assigns assessing current profitability and operational efficiency to a question about component importance, and assigns component importance to a question about current profitability and operational efficiency.
Incorrect: it assigns identifying reasons for change to a question about debt repayment and liquidity, and assigns debt repayment and liquidity to a question about reasons for change.
Correct: IV concerns current profitability and operational efficiency; I concerns relative importance of components; II concerns reasons for change; and III concerns debt repayment and liquidity.

body:
A firm’s existing partners change their profit-sharing ratio without admitting or retiring a partner. The firm undertakes revaluation of its assets and reassessment of its liabilities. Arrange the following steps in the order in which the revaluation adjustment is completed:
(A) Transfer the final balance of the Revaluation Account to the old partners’ capital accounts in their old profit-sharing ratio.
(B) Identify assets and liabilities requiring value changes, including any unrecorded items.
(C) Record revaluation gains and losses in the Revaluation Account.
(D) Determine whether the Revaluation Account has a credit or debit balance.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: First identify the changes in asset and liability values, including unrecorded items, and record the resulting gains or losses in the Revaluation Account. Then determine its balance and transfer that balance to the old partners’ capital accounts in their old profit-sharing ratio. The stated treatment also applies when existing partners change their ratio without admission or retirement.
evidence_quotes: At times there may also be some unrecorded assets and liabilities of the firm. These also have to be brought into the books of the firm. For this purpose the firm has to prepare the Revaluation Account. The gain or loss on revaluation of each asset and liability is transferred to this account and finally its balance is transferred to the capital accounts of the old partners in their old profit sharing ratio.
Any change, in the profit sharing ratio, like admission of partner, may also involve adjustments in respect of revaluation of assets and liabilities
stated_assumptions: The firm’s existing partners change their profit-sharing ratio without admitting or retiring a partner.
The firm undertakes revaluation and reassessment, and any unrecorded assets or liabilities are to be brought into the books.
The sequence requested is for completing the revaluation adjustment, with any final balance transferred to the old partners in their old profit-sharing ratio.
option_analysis: A is incorrect because it determines the Revaluation Account balance before recording the gains and losses.
B is incorrect because it records gains and losses before identifying the valuation changes and unrecorded items.
C is correct: identify the items, record the gains and losses, determine the balance, and transfer it to the old partners in their old ratio.
D is incorrect because it transfers the balance before determining whether the Revaluation Account has a credit or debit balance.

The excerpts establish the valuation assessment, recording of gains and losses, and final transfer of the account balance; they also say these adjustments apply when existing partners change their ratio.
The other options put balance determination before recording, recording before identifying the items, or transfer before determining the balance.

2.7 Revaluation of Assets and Reassessment of Liabilities At the time of admission of a new partner, it is always desirable to ascertain whether the assets of the firm are shown in books at their current values. In case the assets are overstated or understated, these are revalued. Similarly, a reassessment of the liabilities is also done so that these are brought in the books at their correct values. At times there may also be some unrecorded assets and liabilities of the firm. These also have to be brought into the books of the firm. For this purpose the firm has to prepare the Revaluation Account. The gain or loss on revaluation of each

asset and liability is transferred to this account and finally its balance is transferred to the capital accounts of the old partners in their old profit sharing ratio. In other words, the revaluation Reprint 2026-27
PAGE 31
78 Accountancy – Partnership Accounts account is credited with increase in the value of each asset and decrease in its liabilities because it is a gain and is debited with decrease in the value of assets and increase in its liabilities is debited to revaluation account because it is a loss. Similarly unrecorded assets are credited and unrecorded liabilities are debited to the revaluation account. If the revaluation

account finally shows a credit balance then it indicates net gain and if there is a debit balance then it indicates net loss. Which will be transferred to the capital accounts of the old partners in old ratio. The journal entries recorded for revaluation of assets and reassessment of liabilities are as follows: (i) For increase in the value of an asset Asset A/c Dr. To Revaluation A/c (Gain) (ii) For reduction in the value of an asset Revaluation A/c Dr.

body:
An analyst is preparing a common-size statement of profit and loss for each year to compare the expenditure structure of two firms of different sizes. The figures are:
Firm A — Year 1: revenue from operations ₹10,00,000; total expenditure ₹8,00,000. Year 2: revenue from operations ₹16,00,000; total expenditure ₹12,00,000.
Firm B — Year 1: revenue from operations ₹20,00,000; total expenditure ₹14,00,000. Year 2: revenue from operations ₹24,00,000; total expenditure ₹18,00,000.
Using each year's revenue from operations as the base for that year's expenditure percentage, which conclusion is correct?
options: Firm A: 20% to 25%; Firm B: 30% to 25%; the expenditure share rises in A and falls in B.
Firm A: 75% to 80%; Firm B: 75% to 70%; the expenditure share rises in A and falls in B.
Firm A: 80% to 75%; Firm B: 70% to 75%; the expenditure share falls in A and rises in B, although expenditure in rupees rises in both.
Firm A: 80% to 120%; Firm B: 70% to 90%; Year 2 expenditure is divided by Year 1 revenue in each firm.
explanation: For each year, expenditure as a percentage of revenue from operations is expenditure ÷ revenue from operations × 100. Firm A's percentages are 80% and 75%; Firm B's are 70% and 75%. Thus A's expenditure share falls while B's rises, even though the expenditure amount increases for both firms.
evidence_quotes: In the common size statement of profit and loss, the items of expenditure are shown as a percentage of the revenue from operations.
Common size analysis is of immense use for comparing enterprises which differ substantially in size as it provides an insight into the structure of financial statements.
stated_assumptions: The Year 1 and Year 2 figures are paired as labelled, and total expenditure is the item being expressed as a percentage.
Each year's revenue from operations is the base for that same year's expenditure percentage.

The supplied excerpts support common-size statements but do not establish cash-flow-statement procedures; this item therefore assesses a numerical case application of common-size statements instead of cash-flow adjustments.
option_analysis: A uses percentages that do not equal total expenditure divided by revenue from operations for either firm; it does not give the required common-size expenditure percentages.
B gives the correct percentages in reverse year order, so its stated directions of change do not follow the labelled periods.
C correctly calculates each year's expenditure as a percentage of that year's revenue from operations and identifies the resulting trends.
D uses Year 1 revenue as the denominator for Year 2, rather than the corresponding Year 2 revenue from operations.

body: A company issues debentures with a nominal value of ₹100 each for ₹110 each. Considering only the premium on issue, which account is credited with the ₹10 premium per debenture?
options: Discount on Issue of Debentures A/c
explanation: The issue price of ₹110 exceeds the nominal value of ₹100 by ₹10, so the debentures are issued at a premium. The premium is credited to Securities Premium Reserve A/c.
evidence_quotes: The amount of premium is credited to Securities Premium Reserve account and is shown on the liabilities side of the balance sheet under the head “Reserves and Surpluses”.
stated_assumptions: Each debenture has a nominal value of ₹100 and is issued for ₹110.
Only the premium arising on issue is being considered.
option_analysis: A is incorrect: the stated treatment credits the premium to Securities Premium Reserve A/c, not Debentures A/c.
B is correct: the premium on issue is credited to Securities Premium Reserve A/c.
C is incorrect: this is the account associated with a discount on issue, not the premium in the stem.
D is incorrect: the premium is credited to Securities Premium Reserve A/c, not Bank A/c.

body: On dissolution, a firm has ₹4,20,000 cash available from realised assets. It owes ₹1,20,000 to outside creditors, ₹2,80,000 as a partner loan to K and ₹1,20,000 as a partner loan to M. These are the only amounts payable, and there are no unpaid realisation expenses or partner contributions. Outside creditors are paid before partner loans, and the remaining cash is insufficient to pay both partner loans in full. How much should be paid to M against his partner loan?
explanation: After paying the outside creditors, ₹3,00,000 remains for partner loans totalling ₹4,00,000. Since the available balance is inadequate to pay these loans in full, they are paid proportionately. M receives ₹3,00,000 × (₹1,20,000 ÷ ₹4,00,000) = ₹90,000.
evidence_quotes: (i) In paying the debts of the firm to the third parties; (ii) In paying each partner proportionately what is due to him/her from the firm for advances as distinguished from capital (i.e. partner’ loan);
stated_assumptions: ₹4,20,000 is the entire cash available for settlement after realisation.
The stated creditors and partner loans are the only amounts payable, and no realisation expenses remain unpaid.
No partner contributes additional funds to meet a deficiency.
Outside creditors are paid before partner loans; where the available balance cannot fully pay the partner loans, those loans are settled proportionately.
option_analysis: Correct: ₹3,00,000 remains after paying creditors, and M's share of the total partner loans is ₹1,20,000 ÷ ₹4,00,000, giving ₹90,000.
This pays M's full loan, but the cash remaining for both partner loans is only ₹3,00,000 against total loans of ₹4,00,000.
This divides the remaining cash equally between the two partners instead of allocating it in proportion to their loan balances.
This applies K's loan fraction, ₹2,80,000 ÷ ₹4,00,000, to the remaining cash instead of using M's loan fraction.

body:
A company receives applications for more shares than it offered. Match each description of the directors’ approach or the accounting perspective with the corresponding statement.

List-I
(A) Some applications are accepted in full and the others are rejected
(B) A pro-rata allotment is made to all applicants
(C) The directors combine the two approaches described in (A) and (B)
(D) Accounting perspective on when and within which process over-subscription is resolved

List-II
(I) Shares are allotted to all applicants proportionately
(II) Full acceptance and rejection are used together with pro-rata allotment
(III) It is resolved with allotment and considered within the application-and-allotment process
(IV) Selected applications are accepted in full, and the others are rejected

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: The first approach is to accept some applications in full and reject the others, while the second is to allot shares proportionately to all applicants. The third approach combines those two alternatives. Over-subscription is resolved with allotment and is considered within the application-and-allotment process, giving the mapping in option B.
evidence_quotes: they can accept some applications in full and totally reject the others;
they can make a pro-rata allotment to all;
they can adopt a combination of the above two alternatives which happens to be the most common course adopted in practice.

The problem of over subscription is resolved with the allotment of shares. Therefore, from the accounting point of view, it is better to place the situation of over subscription within the total frame of application and allotment, i.e. receipt of application amount, amount due on allotment and its receipt from the shareholders, and the same has been observed in the pattern of entries.
stated_assumptions: Each List-I entry is to be matched with one distinct List-II entry.
The descriptions concern the over-subscription alternatives and accounting perspective stated in the supplied excerpt.
option_analysis: Incorrect: it assigns the combined approach to pro-rata allotment and pro-rata allotment to the combination.
Correct: each description is matched with the corresponding alternative or accounting perspective.
Incorrect: it matches the accounting perspective to full acceptance and rejection, and full acceptance and rejection to the accounting perspective.
Incorrect: it assigns the accounting perspective to pro-rata allotment and pro-rata allotment to the accounting perspective.
subject: accountancy
topic: Financial Analysis: Meaning, Significance, Purpose and Limitations.

reasons: The matches are (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), and (D)-(III), so option B is correct.

E2.1 gives the three directors’ alternatives: full acceptance with rejection, pro-rata allotment to all, and a combination. E2.2 states that oversubscription is resolved with allotment and is considered within the application-and-allotment process.
The other options misassign at least one description; no numerical calculation or additional case assumption is needed.
Quality score 8/10

body:
Consider the following statements about goodwill under the Average Profits Method:
(A) Goodwill is calculated by multiplying average past profits by the agreed number of years’ purchase.
(B) Goodwill is calculated by dividing average past profits by the agreed number of years’ purchase.
(C) The method is based on the assumption that a new business will not be able to earn profits during its first few years of operations.
(D) This method always gives the same goodwill value as every other method.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: The Average Profits Method calculates goodwill by multiplying average past profits by the agreed number of years’ purchase, so (A) is correct. It is also based on the stated assumption about a new business not earning profits in its first few years, so (C) is correct. Statement (B) reverses the multiplication, while (D) conflicts with the fact that goodwill calculated by different methods may differ.
evidence_quotes: Under this method, the goodwill is valued at agreed number of ‘years’ purchase of the average profits of the past few years.
It is based on the assumption that a new business will not be able to earn any profits during the first few years of its operations.
stated_assumptions: The method being considered is the Average Profits Method.
The number of years’ purchase is agreed, as specified in the method description.
option_analysis: Incorrect: statements (B) and (D) are not correct; (B) reverses the stated multiplication, and (D) conflicts with the excerpt’s statement that goodwill values under different methods may differ.
Incorrect: it includes (B), which reverses the stated multiplication, and omits (A), which gives the method’s calculation.
Correct: both (A) and (C) match the stated calculation and assumption of the Average Profits Method.
Incorrect: (D) is inconsistent with the excerpt stating that goodwill calculated by one method may differ from goodwill calculated by another method.

(A) Allow interest on capital: debit Interest on Capital A/c and credit the partners’ Capital/Current A/cs.
(B) Transfer net profit: debit Profit and Loss A/c and credit Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c.
(C) Transfer interest on capital: debit Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c and credit Interest on Capital A/c.
Choose the correct sequence.
explanation: The Profit and Loss Appropriation Account starts with the transfer of net profit. The interest on capital is then allowed to the partners and subsequently transferred to the Appropriation Account. Therefore, the sequence is (B), (A), (C).
evidence_quotes: It starts with the net profit/net loss as per Profit and Loss Account.

body: After the accounts for a year have been prepared and the profit distributed, A, B and C discover that the deed-provided salary to A and interest on capital for all three partners were omitted. The firm decides to correct the omission without altering the old accounts and chooses the direct method rather than a Profit and Loss Adjustment Account. Where should it make the adjustment?
options: Directly in the capital accounts of the concerned partners.
In a Profit and Loss Adjustment Account, followed by transfer to the partners.
In the old Profit and Loss Account, by revising the year’s final accounts.
In the firm’s cash account, without adjusting the partners’ capital accounts.
explanation: For omissions discovered after the accounts have been prepared and profit distributed, the stated alternatives include a Profit and Loss Adjustment Account or direct adjustment in the capital accounts of the concerned partners. Since the firm chooses the direct method, the adjustment should be made in those capital accounts.
evidence_quotes: Instead of altering old accounts, necessary adjustments can be made either; (a) through ‘Profit and Loss Adjustment Account’, or (b) directly in the capital accounts of the concerned partners.
The omission may be in respect of interest on capitals, interest on drawings, interest on partners’ loan, partner’s salary, partner’s commission or outstanding expenses.
stated_assumptions: The stated net profit of ₹2,40,000 is before the omitted salary and interest appropriations.
For the omitted year, A’s salary and all three stated interest amounts are appropriated before the residual profit is shared in the stated 3:2:1 ratio.
The original distribution was made in the 3:2:1 ratio, and no other item needs adjustment.
The firm elects to correct the omission directly through the partners’ capital accounts without altering the old accounts.
option_analysis: Incorrect: it reverses the required direction of the adjustments, since A received less than the correct entitlement while B and C received more.
Correct: A is under-credited by ₹9,000, while B and C are over-credited by ₹6,000 and ₹3,000 respectively.
Incorrect: it omits C’s ₹3,000 over-credit and consequently does not fully adjust A’s under-credit.
Incorrect: it charges B for the entire ₹9,000, although C was also over-credited by ₹3,000.

body: A firm's accounting year runs from 1 January to 31 December. Its last balance sheet was prepared on 30 June, and a partner died on 31 October. Which interval is relevant for accounting for the deceased partner's share of profit or loss, interest on capital and, where applicable, interest on drawings in the partner's claim?
explanation: The deceased partner’s claim accounts for the stated items from the date of the last balance sheet to the date of death. Here, those dates are 30 June and 31 October, making option D correct.
evidence_quotes: Hence, in case of a partner, his claim shall also include his share of profit or loss, interest on capital, interest on drawings (if any) from the date of the last Balance Sheet to the date of his death
stated_assumptions: The accounting year runs from 1 January to 31 December.
The last balance sheet was prepared on 30 June.
The partner died on 31 October.
Interest on capital and interest on drawings are applicable; the item asks for the relevant interval, not the amount of any adjustment.
option_analysis: A is before the date of the last balance sheet and does not cover the interval up to the partner’s death.
B ends on the date of the last balance sheet and does not cover the interval up to the partner’s death.
C begins after the partner’s death.
D runs from the date of the last balance sheet to the date of the partner’s death.

The following deductions, if any, may have to be made from his share: (i) debit balance of his current account (if any); (ii) his share of goodwill to be written off, if necessary; (iii) his share of accumulated losses; (iv) his share of loss on revaluation of assets and liabilities; (v) his share of loss up to the date of retirement/death; (vi) his drawings up to the date of

retirement/death; (vii) interest on drawings, if involved, up to the date of retirement/death. Thus, similar to admission, the various accounting aspects involved on retirement or death of a partner are as follows: 1. Ascertainment of new profit sharing ratio and gaining ratio; 2. Treatment of goodwill; 3. Revaluation of assets and liabilities; 4. Adjustment in respect of unrecorded assets and liabilities; 5. Distribution of accumulated profits and losses; 6.

3.9 Death of a Partner As stated earlier, the accounting treatment in the event of death of a partner is similar to that in case of retirement of a partner, and that in case of death of a partner his claim is transferred to his executors and settled in the same manner as that of the retired partner. However, there is one major difference that, while the retirement normally takes place at the end of an accounting period, the death of a partner may occur any time. Hence, in case of a partner, his claim shall also include his share of profit or loss, interest on capital, interest on drawings (if any) from the date of the last Balance Sheet to

the date of his death of these, the main problem relates to the calculation of profit for the intervening period (i.e., the period from date of the last balance sheet and the date of the partner’s death. Since, it is Reprint 2026-27

body: A company purchases a business from a vendor and settles the entire purchase price by issuing fully paid shares to that vendor. No cash is paid to the vendor. In the same period, the company receives application money in cash from public applicants for a separate share issue. How should the shares issued to the vendor be classified?
options: An issue of shares for consideration other than cash
An issue of shares for cash collected solely on application
An issue of shares for cash collected solely on allotment
An issue of shares for cash collected solely on calls
explanation: The vendor receives fully paid shares as payment for the business, so those shares are issued for consideration other than cash. The cash application money relates to a separate share issue and does not change the classification of the vendor shares.
evidence_quotes: Shares are said to be issued for consideration other than cash when a company purchases business, or some asset/assets, and the vendors have agreed to receive payment in the form of fully paid shares of a company.
When shares are issued for cash, the amount on them can be collected at one or more of the following stages: (i) Application for shares (ii) Allotment of shares (iii) Call/Calls on shares.
stated_assumptions: Only the shares issued to the vendor are being classified.
The vendor receives fully paid shares as the entire consideration for the business, and no cash is paid to the vendor.
The public applicants' cash application money relates to a separate share issue.
option_analysis: Correct: the vendor receives fully paid shares in settlement for the purchased business, which is consideration other than cash.
Incorrect: this describes a cash issue collected solely on application, but no cash is paid for the vendor shares.
Incorrect: this describes a cash issue collected solely on allotment, but no cash is paid for the vendor shares.
Incorrect: this describes a cash issue collected solely on calls, but no cash is paid for the vendor shares.

body:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Activity ratios
(B) Inventory turnover ratio
(C) Higher activity turnover ratio
(D) Low inventory turnover

List-II
(I) Indicates the number of times inventory is converted into revenue from operations during an accounting period
(II) May be due to bad buying or obsolete inventory and is a danger signal
(III) Indicates the speed at which business activities are performed
(IV) Indicates better utilisation of assets and improved efficiency and profitability

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Activity ratios indicate the speed at which business activities are performed. Inventory turnover indicates how many times inventory is converted into revenue from operations during the accounting period. Higher activity turnover indicates better asset utilisation and improved efficiency and profitability, whereas low inventory turnover may signal bad buying or obsolete inventory.
evidence_quotes: These ratios indicate the speed at which, activities of the business are being performed.
It determines the number of times inventory is converted into revenue from operations during the accounting period under consideration.
Higher turnover ratio means better utilisation of assets and signifies improved efficiency and profitability, and as such are known as efficiency ratios.
Low turnover of inventory may be due to bad buying, obsolete inventory, etc., and is a danger signal.
option_analysis: Correct: Activity ratios are matched with the speed of business activities; the remaining pairs correctly describe inventory turnover, higher activity turnover and low inventory turnover.
Incorrect: It assigns the interpretation of higher activity turnover to inventory turnover and the inventory-conversion description to higher activity turnover.
Incorrect: It swaps the descriptions of activity ratios and inventory turnover.
Incorrect: It swaps the stated implications of higher activity turnover and low inventory turnover.

supporting_spans.quote: 213Accounting Ratios 5.8 Activity (or Turnover) Ratio These ratios indicate the speed at which, activities of the business are being performed. The activity ratios express the number of times assets employed, or, for that matter, any constituent of assets, is turned into sales during an accounting period. Higher turnover ratio means better utilisation of assets and signifies improved efficiency and profitability, and as such are known as efficiency ratios. The important activity ratios calculated under this category are 1. Inventory Turnover; 2. Trade receivable Turnover; 3. Trade payable Turnover; 4. Investment (Net assets) Turnover 5. Fixed

assets Turnover; and 6. Working capital Turnover. 5.8.1 Inventory Turnover Ratio It determines the number of times inventory is converted into revenue from operations during the accounting period under consideration. It expresses the relationship between the cost of revenue from operations and average inventory. The formula for its calculation is as follows: Inventory Turnover Ratio = Cost of Revenue from Operations / Average Inventory Where average inventory refers to arithmetic average of opening and closing inventory, and the cost of revenue from operations means revenue from operations less gross profit. Significance : It studies the

frequency of conversion of inventory of finished goods into revenue from operations. It is also a measure of liquidity. It determines how many times inventory is purchased or replaced during a year. Low turnover of inventory may be due to bad buying, obsolete inventory, etc., and is a danger signal. High turnover is good but it must be carefully interpreted as it may be due to buying in small lots or selling quickly at low margin to realise cash. Thus, it throws light on utilisation of inventory of goods. Reprint 2026-27

body:

(A) The existing partners and the incoming partner cannot specifically decide the method.
(B) The existing partners and the incoming partner may specifically decide the method.

body: P and Q continue as partners in a firm, with no admission or retirement. They revise their profit-sharing ratio, under which P sacrifices a share and Q gains a share. A goodwill adjustment is required. Which treatment correctly records this adjustment?
options: Credit P’s Capital Account and debit Q’s Capital Account.
Debit P’s Capital Account and credit Q’s Capital Account.
Credit both P’s and Q’s Capital Accounts.
Debit both P’s and Q’s Capital Accounts.
explanation: The stated principle is to credit the sacrificing partner and debit the gaining partner for the goodwill adjustment. P sacrifices and Q gains, so P’s Capital Account is credited and Q’s Capital Account is debited.
evidence_quotes: This is done by crediting sacrificing partner's and debiting gaining partner's with appropriate amounts
stated_assumptions: There is no admission or retirement of a partner.
P is a sacrificing partner and Q is a gaining partner under the revised ratio.

Incorrect: This reverses the required treatment for the sacrificing and gaining partners.

Incorrect: The required treatment credits the sacrificing partner and debits the gaining partner, not both partners.

topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership firm

body: A company reports the following figures: total assets are ₹24 lakh in Year 1 and ₹15 lakh in Year 2; inventories are ₹5 lakh in Year 1 and ₹4 lakh in Year 2. What percentage of total assets is represented by Year 1 inventories in a common-size balance sheet? Give your answer to two decimal places.
explanation: In a common-size balance sheet, an asset is expressed as a percentage of total assets. For Year 1 inventories, (₹5 lakh ÷ ₹24 lakh) × 100 = 20.83%. The other figures result from mixing years or calculating the change in inventory instead of its share of total assets.
evidence_quotes: For example, a common size balance sheet shows the percentage of each asset to the total assets, and that of each liability to the total liabilities.
stated_assumptions: The stated inventory and total-assets figures apply to the respective years.
Use total assets for the relevant year as the common-size balance-sheet base.
Report the result to two decimal places.
option_analysis: A is incorrect because it divides Year 2 inventory by Year 1 total assets.
B is correct: Year 1 inventory of ₹5 lakh divided by Year 1 total assets of ₹24 lakh, multiplied by 100, is 20.83%.
C is incorrect because it gives the decrease in inventory as a percentage of Year 1 inventory, not inventory as a percentage of total assets.
D is incorrect because it divides Year 1 inventory by Year 2 total assets.

topic: Financial Statements of a Company : Preparation of simple financial statements of a company in the prescribed form with major headings and sub headings.

A, C and D do not equal the required Year 1 inventory-to-Year 1 total-assets percentage; only B is correct.

supporting_spans.quote: 182 Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements II.Assets 1) Non-current assets a) Fixed assets - Tangible assets 14 8 - Intangible assets 3 2 2) Current assets a) Inventories 5 4 b) Cash and cash equivalents 2 1 Total 24 15 4.6 Common Size Statement Common Size Statement, also known as component percentage statement, is a financial tool for studying the key changes and trends in the financial position and operational result of a company. Here, each item in the statement is stated as a percentage of the aggregate, or revenue from operations of which that item is a part. For example, a common size balance sheet shows

the percentage of each asset to the total assets, and that of each liability to the total liabilities. Similarly, in the common size statement of profit and loss, the items of expenditure are shown as a percentage of the revenue from operations. If such a statement is prepared for successive periods, it shows the changes of the respective percentages over a period of time. Common size analysis is of immense use for comparing enterprises which differ substantially in size as it provides an insight into the structure of financial statements. Inter-firm comparison or comparison of the company’s position with the related industry as a whole is

possible with the help of common size statement analysis. The following procedure may be adopted for preparing the common size statements. 1. List out absolute figures in rupees at two points of time, say year 1, and year 2 (Column 2 & 4 of Exhibit 4.2). 2. Choose a common base (as 100). For example, revenue from operations may be taken as base (100) in case of statement of profit and loss and total assets or total liabilities (100) in case of balance sheet. 3. For all items of Col. 2 and 3 work out the percentage of that total. Column 4 and 5 shows these percentages in Exhibit 4.2. Common Size Statement Particulars Year Y ear Percentage

body:
Match List-I with List-II using the terms defined here: an issue price equal to nominal value is at par, above nominal value is at a premium, and below nominal value is at a discount. A redemption amount equal to nominal value is redeemable at par; an amount above nominal value is redeemable at a premium. All amounts are per debenture.

List-I
(A) Nominal value ₹1,000; issue price ₹1,000; redemption amount ₹1,000
(B) Nominal value ₹1,000; issue price ₹1,100; redemption amount ₹1,000
(C) Nominal value ₹1,000; issue price ₹1,000; redemption amount ₹1,100
(D) Nominal value ₹1,000; issue price ₹900; redemption amount ₹1,100

List-II
(I) Issued at par and redeemable at par
(II) Issued at a discount and redeemable at a premium
(III) Issued at par and redeemable at a premium
(IV) Issued at a premium and redeemable at par

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Compare each issue price and redemption amount with its nominal value. (A) is at par for issue and redemption; (B) is issued at a premium and redeemable at par; (C) is issued at par and redeemable at a premium; and (D) is issued at a discount and redeemable at a premium. List-I
(A) Estimating funds required for long-term assets
(B) Estimating when funds must be available
(C) Specifying possible sources of funds
(D) Dealing with surplus funds
List-II
(I) Put the surplus to the best possible use
(II) Identify where funds may be obtained
(III) Determine the time when funds are needed
(IV) Estimate the amount required for long-term assets
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Financial planning estimates the amount of funds required for purposes such as long-term assets, when funds must be available, and possible sources of funds. It also aims to avoid unnecessary funding by putting surplus funds to the best possible use, so the matching in option C is correct.

body: A firm’s employees joined for different reasons: some value competitive salaries, others peer recognition, and others personal growth. The employees are expected to contribute to one common organisational goal. The manager accommodates their differing personal goals and arranges their work so that each person’s effort supports that common goal. Which conclusion best describes coordination in this situation?
options: It directs diverse individual efforts towards a common goal without requiring employees to have identical personal purposes.
It requires employees to adopt identical personal purposes before they can work towards a common goal.
It fulfils the firm’s social obligation by creating benefits for the community.
It replaces the common organisational goal with separate goals for employees’ financial, social and growth needs.
explanation: The employees have different purposes, yet their efforts are directed towards a common organisational goal. Coordination involves teamwork and directing individual effort in a common direction; it does not require identical personal purposes. The excerpts distinguish this from social objectives and from the reconciliation of personal goals with organisational objectives.
evidence_quotes: This requires team work and coordination of individual effort in a common direction.
Management has to reconcile personal goals with organisational objectives for harmony in the organisation.
stated_assumptions: The employees have differing personal purposes but are expected to contribute to the stated common organisational goal.
The manager's arrangement directs each employee's effort towards that shared goal.
option_analysis: A. Correct: it describes coordination of individual effort in a common direction while allowing members to have different purposes.
B. Incorrect: the employees in the stem have different purposes, and the excerpt states that members with different purposes work towards a common organisational goal.
C. Incorrect: creating benefits for society describes a social objective, not the coordination of employees' efforts towards the stated organisational goal.
D. Incorrect: the excerpt describes reconciling personal goals with organisational objectives, not replacing the common organisational goal with separate personal goals.

body: A company prepares a chart that names each employee's immediate superior and reporting channel. After the chart is shared, employees know whom to approach with work-related questions. No tasks are redistributed, and no change in resource use or organisational size is described. Which importance of organising is most directly illustrated?
explanation: Organising leads to clarity in reporting relationships. In this case, employees learn whom to approach because their reporting channels are specified. The case does not describe a redistribution of tasks, a change in resource use or growth in organisational size.
evidence_quotes: Organising is considered important because it leads to division of work, clarity in reporting relationships, optimum utilization of resources, growth, better administration and greater creativity.
stated_assumptions: The chart specifying immediate superiors and reporting channels is the only organisational change described.
The question asks for the importance of organising most directly shown by the stated outcome.
option_analysis: A is correct because the stated outcome is that employees know whom to approach, illustrating clarity in reporting relationships.
B is incorrect because the case explicitly says tasks are not redistributed.
C is incorrect because the case states that no change in resource use is described.
D is incorrect because the case states that no change in organisational size is described.

body:
A firm has manufactured a product. It completes packaging, branding, pricing and promotion before dispatching the product. In this workflow, physical movement from the place of production to the place of distribution is completed before the product is recorded as available to customers. Treat each description below as a separate stage and arrange the stages from first to last.
(A) The product is available to customers at the right place, in the right quantity and at the right time.
(B) The product is manufactured.
(C) The product is packaged, branded, priced and promoted.
(D) The product is physically handled and moved from production to distribution.
Choose the correct sequence from the options below:
explanation: Manufacturing comes first, followed by packaging, branding, pricing and promotion, as stated in the stem. The excerpt describes physical distribution as the movement of goods from production to distribution, and the stem specifies that this movement precedes customer availability. The resulting order is (B), (C), (D), (A).
evidence_quotes: Once goods are manufactured, packaged, branded, priced, and promoted, these must be made available to customers at the ri ght place, in right quantity and at the right time.
The physical handling and movement of goods from place of production to the place of distribution is referred to as physical distribution, which is a very important element of marketing mix.
stated_assumptions: The stem treats manufacturing, product preparation, physical movement and customer availability as separate stages.
Packaging, branding, pricing and promotion are completed after manufacture and before dispatch.
Physical movement is completed before the product is recorded as available to customers.
No additional stages, such as storage or channel selection, are included in the sequence.
option_analysis: Incorrect: this places physical movement before packaging, branding, pricing and promotion, although the stem states that preparation is completed before dispatch.
Correct: it places manufacture before preparation, preparation before physical movement, and physical movement before customer availability.
Incorrect: this places packaging, branding, pricing and promotion before manufacture, contrary to the workflow stated in the stem.
Incorrect: this places customer availability before physical movement, contrary to the workflow stated in the stem.

Once goods are manufactured, packaged, branded, priced, and promoted, these must be made available to customers at the ri ght place, in right quantity and at the right time. For example, a person convinced about the quality, etc. of a product, say, a detergent bar, wants to purchase the same. He/She goes to a retail outlet and asks for the product. If that product is not available in that shop, he/she may purchase some of the alternative brand available. This way a sure sale is lost because goods were not available at the place where the customer wanted to purchase.

Thus, it is an important responsibility of the marketers to make the product physically available at a place where the customers would like them to buy. body: Employees in an organisation may have personal goals, while the organisation has its own objectives. Which management action is identified as promoting harmony between them?
options: Create benefits for society through production methods and community support.
Reconcile employees’ personal goals with the organisation’s objectives.
Formulate overall organisational goals and strategies to achieve them.
Directly oversee workers’ efforts to maintain output quality and reduce material wastage.
explanation: Reconciling personal goals with organisational objectives promotes harmony in the organisation. Option A describes social objectives, while options C and D describe responsibilities of top management and supervisory management, respectively.
evidence_quotes: Management has to reconcile personal goals with organisational objectives for harmony in the organisation.

option_analysis: A is incorrect because it describes creating benefits for society, which is a social objective.
B is correct because reconciling personal goals with organisational objectives promotes harmony.
C is incorrect because formulating overall organisational goals and strategies is a responsibility of top management.
D is incorrect because directly overseeing workforce efforts is a responsibility of supervisory management.

body:
An organisation is formulating a strategy. Consider the following statements:
(A) The business environment needs to be considered while formulating the strategy.
(B) Changes in the economic, political, social, legal and technological environment affect the organisation’s strategy.
(C) Considering the business environment replaces the need to determine long-term objectives and allocate resources.
(D) The business environment needs to be considered only if the organisation plans to enter a new line of business.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

body:
Arrange the following stages in the order in which staffing responsibility is described as an organisation moves from a small organisation to a larger one:
(A) Managers in a small organisation may handle employees’ salaries, welfare and working conditions.
(B) The organisation grows and the number of persons employed increases.
(C) A separate human resource department is formed.
(D) Specialists in that department manage people.
Choose the correct sequence:
explanation: At the small scale, managers may handle duties related to employees’ salaries, welfare and working conditions. As the organisation grows and employs more people, a separate human resource department is formed, with specialists to manage people. The resulting order is (A)-(B)-(C)-(D).
evidence_quotes: In small organisations, managers may perform all duties related to employees salaries, welfare and working conditions. But as organisations grow and number of persons employed increases, a separate department called the human resource department is formed which has specialists in the field to manage people.
stated_assumptions: The sequence describes a progression from a small-organisation arrangement to a larger-organisation arrangement.
The listed stages include only the organisational-scale progression described in the question; no additional staffing stages are assumed.
option_analysis: Option A puts organisational growth before the small-organisation arrangement, reversing the scale progression specified in the question.
Option B places formation of the human resource department before organisational growth and the increase in employees that precede its formation in the stated progression.
Option C places specialists managing people before the separate department in which the excerpt says they work is formed.
Option D correctly orders the small-organisation arrangement, growth in size and employee numbers, formation of the department, and specialist management.

body:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I
(A) Interest Coverage Ratio (ICR)
(B) Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR)
(C) Return on Investment (RoI)
(D) Cost of debt
List-II
(I) A higher value indicates lower risk of failing to meet interest payments, but this measure does not capture a low cash balance or repayment obligations.
(II) Cash profits from operations are compared with the total cash required to service debt and preference share capital; this measure addresses the stated deficiencies of the interest-based ratio.
(III) A higher value can support the use of trading on equity to increase EPS; this factor concerns the company’s return from investment.
(IV) A lower rate at which the firm can borrow increases its capacity to employ debt.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: ICR measures how many times EBIT covers interest, and a higher ratio indicates lower risk of failing to meet interest payments, though it does not account for low cash balances or repayment obligations. DSCR compares operating cash profits with the total cash required for debt and preference-share service. RoI relates to the use of trading on equity to increase EPS, whereas a lower cost of debt increases the capacity to employ debt; hence the correct mapping is option C.
evidence_quotes: The interest coverage ratio refers to the number of times earnings before interest and taxes of a company covers the interest obligation.
A firm may have a high EBIT but low cash balance. Apart from interest, repayment obligations are also relevant.
The cash profits generated by the operations are compared with the total cash required for the service of the debt and the preference share capital.
A firm’s ability to borrow at a lower rate increases its capacity to employ higher debt.
stated_assumptions: The supplied reference supports factors affecting capital structure, not factors affecting fixed- and working-capital requirements; this item is limited to the capital-structure factors stated in the reference.
Each List-II description is to be matched with the factor whose meaning or effect it describes; no additional facts or numerical values are assumed.
option_analysis: Incorrect: This swaps ICR and DSCR. ICR concerns EBIT covering interest, while DSCR compares operating cash profits with total cash required for debt and preference-share service.
Incorrect: This swaps the effects associated with RoI and cost of debt. RoI relates to trading on equity and EPS; borrowing at a lower rate relates to greater capacity to employ debt.

Correct: ICR matches the interest-payment risk description, DSCR matches the broader debt-service comparison, RoI matches trading on equity and EPS, and cost of debt matches the borrowing-rate effect.
Incorrect: This assigns the DSCR cash-service comparison to RoI and the RoI trading-on-equity effect to DSCR.

topic: Fixed and Working Capital – meaning and factors affecting their requirements.

reasons: ICR matches (I): a higher ratio indicates lower risk of failing to meet interest payments, but does not capture low cash balances or principal repayment obligations (E1.2).
DSCR matches (II): it compares operating cash profits with the cash required to service debt and preference share capital, addressing ICR’s deficiencies (E1.3).
RoI matches (III), and cost of debt matches (IV) (E1.4, E1.5). Thus the complete matching is A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV: option C.
The tested factors are supported as capital-structure considerations, and no case-specific values or assumptions are needed.
Quality score 8/10
quality_notes: A direct, textbook-aligned matching question; it mainly tests recognition of definitions.
The distractors offer plausible mismatches, though the item is relatively straightforward.

Interest Coverage Ratio (ICR): The interest coverage ratio refers to the number of times earnings before interest and taxes of a company covers the interest obligation. This may be calculated as follows: ICR = EBIT Interest The higher the ratio, lower shall be the risk of company failing to meet its interest payment obligations. However, this ratio is not an adequate measure. A firm may have a high EBIT but low cash balance. Apart from interest,

repayment obligations are also relevant. 3. Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR): Debt Service Coverage Ratio takes care of the deficiencies referred to in the Interest Coverage Ratio (ICR). The cash profits generated by the operations are compared with the total cash required for the service of the debt and the preference share capital. It is calculated as follows: Profit after tax + Depreciation + Interest + Non Cash exp. Pref. Div + Interest + Repayment obligation a higher DSCR indicates better ability to meet cash commitments and consequently, the company’s potential to increase debt component in its capital structure. 4. Return on

body:
A marketing description states that goods are manufactured, packaged, branded, priced and promoted before being made available to customers. Arrange the following activities in that order:
(1) Price the product
(2) Make the product available to customers
(3) Manufacture the product
(4) Promote the product
(5) Brand the product
(6) Package the product
explanation: The stated progression is manufacture, packaging, branding, pricing, promotion and then making the goods available to customers. This corresponds to 3, 6, 5, 1, 4, 2.
evidence_quotes: Once goods are manufactured, packaged, branded, priced, and promoted, these must be made available to customers
stated_assumptions: The required order is the progression explicitly stated in the stem.
The six listed activities correspond to the six stages in that progression; no additional activity is to be inserted.
option_analysis: Incorrect: it places branding before packaging, contrary to the stated progression.
Incorrect: it places promotion before pricing, contrary to the stated progression.
Correct: it places manufacture, packaging, branding, pricing and promotion before making the product available to customers.
Incorrect: it makes the product available before promotion, contrary to the stated progression.

body: A country's reserve bank sells foreign exchange as an official reserve transaction solely to bridge a gap in its balance of payments. How should this transaction be classified?
explanation: An official reserve transaction undertaken to bridge a balance of payments gap is an accommodating transaction. Accommodating transactions are classified as below-the-line items.

body:
Consider the following facts: After forty years of planned development, India achieved a strong industrial base and became self-sufficient in the production of food grains. In 1991, a crisis in the balance of payments led to the introduction of economic reforms.

Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Forty years of planned development
(B) Strong industrial base
(C) Self-sufficiency in the production of food grains
(D) 1991 balance-of-payments crisis

List-II
(I) Led to the introduction of economic reforms
(II) Achievement stated for India after planned development
(III) Achievement in food-grain production stated for India
(IV) Period after which the two achievements in (II) and (III) are reported

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
A. (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
B. (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
C. (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
D. (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
explanation: The stem states that the strong industrial base and self-sufficiency in food-grain production were achievements after forty years of planned development. It separately states that the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis led to the introduction of reforms. Therefore, the complete matching is (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(III) and (D)-(I).
evidence_quotes: After forty years of planned development, India has been able to achieve a strong industrial base and became self-sufficient in the production of food grains.
In 1991, a crisis in the balance of payments led to the introduction of economic reforms in the country.
stated_assumptions: The matches are based only on the relationships stated in the stem; no additional goals of planned development are being inferred.
The phrase 'after forty years' identifies the period preceding the two stated achievements and is not used as a calendar-date calculation.
option_analysis: Option A interchanges the descriptions for the industrial-base achievement and food-grain achievement.
Option B assigns the planned-development period to an achievement and the industrial-base achievement to a period.
Option C correctly matches the planned-development period, both stated achievements and the crisis that led to reforms.
Option D assigns the food-grain achievement to the reform trigger and the balance-of-payments crisis to the food-grain achievement.

reasons: The excerpt states that forty years of planned development preceded both achievements: a strong industrial base and self-sufficiency in food grains. Thus A-IV, B-II and C-III; it also states that the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis led to reforms, so D-I. These pairings appear together only in option C.
All decisive facts are explicit in the stimulus and supported by E1.1; no additional case assumptions or calculations are needed.

body: A government reviews two periods. In Period I, aggregate demand is insufficient for full utilisation of labour and other resources, and employment has not recovered automatically because wages and prices do not fall below a certain level. In Period II, aggregate demand exceeds available output while employment is high, and inflation arises. Which pair of responses best represents the government’s stabilisation function in these periods?
options: Reduce aggregate demand in Period I and raise it in Period II.
Rely on automatic recovery in Period I and reduce aggregate demand in Period II.
Raise aggregate demand in both Period I and Period II.
Raise aggregate demand in Period I and reduce it in Period II.
explanation: In Period I, insufficient demand and the stated failure of employment to recover automatically call for government intervention to raise aggregate demand. In Period II, demand exceeds available output under high employment and inflation arises, so restrictive conditions may be used to reduce demand; both responses form part of the stabilisation function.
evidence_quotes: In any period, the level of demand may not be sufficient for full utilisation of labour and other resources of the economy. Since wages and prices do not fall below a level, employment cannot be brought back to the earlier level automatically. The government needs to intervene to raise the aggregate demand.

On the other hand, there may be times when demand exceeds available output under conditions of high employment and thus may give rise to inflation. In such situations, restrictive conditions may be needed to reduce demand.
stated_assumptions: Period I has insufficient aggregate demand and employment has not recovered automatically because wages and prices do not fall below a certain level.
Period II has aggregate demand exceeding available output, high employment and inflation.
The question asks for the government responses indicated for these two periods.
option_analysis: Incorrect: it reverses the indicated response for Period I, where aggregate demand needs to be raised.
Incorrect: the stated conditions in Period I do not support relying on automatic recovery; government intervention to raise aggregate demand is indicated.
Incorrect: the response indicated for Period II is to reduce demand, not raise it.
Correct: it pairs raising aggregate demand in Period I with reducing demand in Period II.

body:
Consider the following statements about the colonial economy of India:
(A) Colonial policies prioritised the economic interests of Britain over the development of the Indian economy.
(B) These policies transformed India into a supplier of raw materials and a consumer of finished industrial products from Britain.
(C) Colonial policies were more concerned with developing India than with protecting and promoting the economic interests of Britain.
(D) India had no manufacturing activities before British rule.
Which of the statements are correct?
explanation: Statements (A) and (B) accurately describe the priority and effect of colonial economic policies. Statements (C) and (D) are incorrect: the policies favoured the home country’s interests, and India had manufacturing activities before British rule.
evidence_quotes: The economic policies pursued by the colonial government in India were concerned more with the protection and promotion of the economic interests of their home country than with the development of the Indian economy.

Such policies brought about a fundamental change in the structure of the Indian economy — transforming the country into supplier of raw materials and consumer of finished industrial products from Britain.
Though agriculture was the main source of livelihood for most people, yet, the country’s economy was characterised by various kinds of manufacturing activities.
stated_assumptions: The statements refer to colonial rule in India.
In statement (A), the colonial government's 'home country' refers to Britain, as identified in statement (B).
option_analysis: Incorrect: statement (A) is correct, but statement (C) reverses the stated priority of colonial policies.
Incorrect: statement (B) is correct, but statement (D) conflicts with the stated presence of manufacturing activities in India before British rule.
Incorrect: both statements (C) and (D) conflict with the stated account.
Correct: both statements (A) and (B) match the stated priority and effect of colonial economic policies.

chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
topic: Main features, problems and policies of agriculture (institutional aspects and new agricultural strategy), industry (IPR 1956; SSI – role & importance) and foreign trade. Unit II Economic Reforms since 1991: Macroeconomics: Meaning.

reasons: A and B are correct: the excerpts describe colonial policy as serving British economic interests and transforming India into a raw-material supplier and a consumer of British finished goods.
C reverses that stated priority. D is false because India had manufacturing activities, including handicraft industries, before British rule.
Thus only (A) and (B) are correct: option D.

body:
Two independent markets, X and Y, are initially in equilibrium. In Market X, the equilibrium price is ₹50 per unit. A price ceiling of ₹40 is imposed; at this price, quantity demanded is 90 units and quantity supplied is 55 units. In Market Y, the equilibrium price is ₹30 per unit. A price floor of ₹36 is imposed; at this price, quantity demanded is 40 units and quantity supplied is 72 units. For each market, calculate the excess-demand gap as quantity demanded minus quantity supplied, or the excess-supply gap as quantity supplied minus quantity demanded, as applicable.
Which option correctly identifies the resulting gaps?
options: Market X: excess demand of 35 units; Market Y: excess supply of 32 units.
Market X: excess supply of 35 units; Market Y: excess demand of 32 units.
Market X: excess demand of 145 units; Market Y: excess supply of 112 units.
Market X: excess demand of 35 units; Market Y: excess demand of 32 units.
explanation: In Market X, the ceiling is below the equilibrium price, and the excess-demand gap is 90 − 55 = 35 units. In Market Y, the floor is above the equilibrium price, and the excess-supply gap is 72 − 40 = 32 units.
evidence_quotes: Imposition of price ceiling below the equilibrium price leads to an excess demand.
Imposition of price floor above the equilibrium price leads to an excess supply.
stated_assumptions: Markets X and Y are independent, and each quantity demanded and supplied is measured at the stated controlled price.
The excess-demand gap is quantity demanded minus quantity supplied; the excess-supply gap is quantity supplied minus quantity demanded.
option_analysis: A is correct: the stated quantities give an excess-demand gap of 35 units in X and an excess-supply gap of 32 units in Y.
B reverses the type of gap in each market, despite the ceiling in X being below equilibrium and the floor in Y being above equilibrium.
C adds the quantities demanded and supplied in each market rather than calculating the difference between them.
D correctly identifies the gap in X but incorrectly labels the gap in Y as excess demand.

body: An economy follows the simplified circular-flow assumptions of no government, no external trade and no saving. Households spend their entire income on goods and services produced by domestic firms. During a period, households receive wages of ₹4,80,000, interest of ₹70,000, profits of ₹1,30,000 and rent of ₹20,000, with no other household income. What is their aggregate consumption expenditure on the domestic firms’ goods and services?
explanation: Households spend their entire income on goods and services produced by domestic firms. Their aggregate income is ₹4,80,000 + ₹70,000 + ₹1,30,000 + ₹20,000 = ₹7,00,000, so aggregate consumption expenditure is ₹7,00,000.
evidence_quotes: In this simplified economy, there is only one way in which the households may dispose off their earnings – by spending their entire income on the goods and services produced by the domestic firms.
The aggregate consumption by the households of the economy is equal to the aggregate expenditure on goods and services produced by the firms in the economy.
stated_assumptions: The economy has no government, external trade or saving.
Households spend their entire income on goods and services produced by domestic firms.
The stated wages, interest, profits and rent are the only household income during the period.
option_analysis: A omits profits: wages, interest and rent total ₹5,70,000.
B omits rent: wages, interest and profits total ₹6,80,000.
C adds all four stated factor incomes, giving ₹7,00,000.
D subtracts interest instead of adding it, giving ₹5,60,000.

body:
For a firm operating in the short run, match each cost concept in List-I with its description in List-II.
List-I
(A) Total fixed cost (TFC)
(B) Total variable cost (TVC)
(C) Total cost (TC)
(D) Short-run marginal cost (SMC)
List-II
(I) The vertical sum of TFC and TVC
(II) Does not change when output changes
(III) The increase in TVC from producing one additional unit
(IV) The sum of marginal costs up to an output level
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: In the short run, TFC does not change with output, while TVC equals the sum of marginal costs up to that output level. TC is the vertical sum of TFC and TVC, and SMC is the increase in TVC from producing one additional unit. These relationships give the mapping in option A.
evidence_quotes: as long as IRS operates, average cost falls as the firm increases output.
the average cost remains constant as long as CRS operates.
as long as DRS operates, the average cost must be rising as the firm increases output.
At the minimum point of the LRAC curve, CRS is observed.
stated_assumptions: The supplied excerpts do not establish the shapes of TP, MP and AP curves, so this item tests the explicitly supported relationship between returns to scale and LRAC.
The minimum-point match refers to the typical firm's LRAC curve described in the supplied excerpt.
option_analysis: Correct: IRS matches falling average cost, CRS matches constant average cost, DRS matches rising average cost, and the LRAC minimum matches CRS.
Incorrect: it assigns constant average cost to IRS and falling average cost to CRS, contrary to the stated relationships.
Incorrect: it assigns rising average cost to CRS and constant average cost to DRS, contrary to the stated relationships.
Incorrect: it matches DRS with the minimum point and the minimum point with rising average cost, whereas the minimum point is associated with CRS.

topic: Shapes of TP, MP and AP curves

The supplied NCERT excerpts support the fixed-cost behaviour, the marginal-cost/TVC relationships, and the vertical-sum definition of TC. The other options misassign at least one of these definitions.

body:
Arrange the following steps in the correct sequence for constructing a market supply curve from the supply schedules of the same firms at a range of market prices.
(A) Add the quantities supplied by all firms at a given market price.
(B) Read the quantity supplied by each firm at that market price.
(C) Repeat the process for other market prices.
(D) Plot the aggregate quantity supplied against the corresponding market price.
explanation: At a given market price, first read each firm's quantity supplied and then add these quantities to find market supply at that price. Repeat this for other prices, then plot aggregate quantities against the corresponding prices to obtain the market supply curve.
evidence_quotes: In other words, the market supply at price p is the summation of the supplies of individual firms at that price.
The market supply curve shows the output levels (plotted on the x-axis) that firms in the market produce in aggregate corresponding to different values of the market price (plotted on the y-axis).
stated_assumptions: The supply schedules of the same firms are available for each market price considered.
The steps are to be carried out one market price at a time.
option_analysis: Incorrect: it adds firm quantities before reading the quantity supplied by each firm at that price.
Correct: it reads each firm's quantity, sums the quantities at that price, repeats for other prices, and plots the resulting aggregate quantities against prices.
Incorrect: it repeats the process for other prices before calculating aggregate supply at the current price.
Incorrect: it starts by adding quantities before reading each firm's supply at a given price.

body: A central bank allows its exchange rate to move and does not hold it at an announced fixed rate. Whenever it considers appropriate, the bank buys or sells foreign currencies to moderate exchange-rate movements. Assume these are the only relevant policy features. Which description correctly identifies the exchange-rate system and the status of official reserve transactions?
options: A flexible exchange-rate system with no central-bank intervention; official reserve transactions equal zero.
A managed floating exchange-rate system with intervention to moderate movements; official reserve transactions are non-zero.
A fixed exchange-rate system with the rate held at an announced level; official reserve transactions are non-zero.
A fixed exchange-rate system with the rate held at an announced level; official reserve transactions equal zero.
explanation: The rate is allowed to move, while the central bank intervenes to moderate its movements; this combination describes managed floating. Under this system, official reserve transactions are not equal to zero. Therefore, B is the only option consistent with both features of the case.
evidence_quotes: It is a mixture of a flexible exchange rate system (the float part) and a fixed rate system (the managed part).
Official reserve transactions are, therefore, not equal to zero.
stated_assumptions: The case treats the stated policy features as complete; there is no fixed exchange-rate commitment.
The central bank's purchases and sales of foreign currencies are interventions intended to moderate exchange-rate movements.
option_analysis: Incorrect: the case includes central-bank intervention, and official reserve transactions under managed floating are not equal to zero.
Correct: the case combines a rate that is allowed to move with intervention to moderate movements, and the reserve transactions are non-zero.
Incorrect: the case states that the rate is not held at an announced fixed level.
Incorrect: the case states that the rate is not held at an announced fixed level, and the intervention means official reserve transactions are not zero.
